newsitem.title: UK: UK TV watchdog upholds complaints against car ads.
newsitem.headline: UK TV watchdog upholds complaints against car ads.

text.p: Britain's television watchdog on Monday said it upheld complaints against three different car commercials and warned that car ads must not condone irresponsible driving.
The Independent Television Commission (ITC), in its monthly report, said it upheld complaints against ads for the Volkswagen Passat, Volkswagen Polo and the Ford Fiesta.
The Volkswagen Polo advert, created by BMP DDB Needham, drew complaints from 144 viewers who objected to its use of violence and human suffering, the ITC said.

The ad, designed to reassure viewers that small cars can offer good accident protection, showed scenes of a fallen jockey in danger from other horses, a fugitive trying to shield himself from snarling police dogs, and a cornered boxer and firemen ducking to avoid a ball of flame. The ITC said the ad should be aired only after the 9 p.m. adult watershed.

The ITC also upheld complaints filed by 44 viewers, a local road safety authority and the Department of Transport against an ad for the VW Passat, also created by BMP DDB Needham. The ad showed a test driver, dressed in crash helmet and overalls, driving a Passat around a test circuit.

The ITC found the ad harmful and said it featured driving that on a public road "would have been aggressive, irresponsible and too fast for the situations shown." It ordered that the ad no longer be broadcast.

The ITC intervened on its own to complain about a Ford Fiesta ad created by Ogilvy & Mather. The ad showed a baby ageing to become an elderly man in 10 seconds. The caption read, "The Fiesta 1.4 does 0-60 in 10.8 seconds." The ITC said it required that the ad cease because television car adverts should not be based on speed, power or acceleration claims.

In addition, the ITC said it ruled that an advert for SmithKline Beecham's Lucozade NRG, a soft drink, was offensive and should not have been broadcast around children's programming. The ad showed an old-style crooner in his rocking chair who, after sipping Lucozade NRG, is transformed into a manic punk-style character and smashes up his room.
The ITC noted that the ad had been restricted from being aired near children's programming and that the complaints upheld related to mis-scheduling.
